text: A single qubit's state is two complex numbers, which is hard to picture. The Bloch sphere maps that state to a single 3D arrow, and once you can read that arrow, every single-qubit gate you've learned becomes a visible rotation instead of an abstract matrix.

For a circuit with no measurement yet applied, you can get the exact statevector and plot it directly: Statevector of qc, then plot_bloch_multivector. For a multi-qubit circuit where the qubits aren't entangled with each other, this draws one small sphere per qubit. If the qubits are entangled, this per-qubit picture breaks down — exactly the limitation next lesson's Q-sphere exists to solve.
Here's real output from Qiskit's own documentation, showing exactly what that rendering looks like — each qubit gets its own arrow on its own sphere.

Five simple one-gate circuits, computed directly from exact statevector amplitudes. No gates leaves the qubit at the north pole. X flips it straight through the center to the south pole — it doesn't nudge the arrow, it flips it. H lands exactly on the equator along positive x, which is the geometric picture of equal superposition — maximally far from both poles. And RY of pi-over-3 lands at roughly 0.866, 0, 0.5 — tilted 60 degrees from the north pole toward positive x.

RX of pi-over-2 lands at 0, negative 1, 0 — x equals zero, meaning it never leaves the y-z plane, while RY never left the x-z plane. Once you know which axis a rotation gate is named after, you know which plane of the sphere it moves the vector within — and that turns the Bloch sphere from a pretty picture into an actual debugging tool. If a gate's output doesn't land in the plane you expected, something in your circuit isn't doing what you think.

The Bloch sphere's hard limit is that it only describes one qubit at a time, and it breaks down entirely for entangled states. Next lesson covers the Q-sphere and state-city plots that exist precisely to cover that gap.
